title: Product Fragmenting Under Growth
summary: Product fragmentation under growth is a structural situation in which new features, flows, markets, modules, or local variants are added without a shared architecture that defines what must remain coherent. The problem affects user experience, engineering work, and organisational coordination.
keyFacts: Fragmentation can emerge without any single feature decision being wrong.
The problem is often invisible inside the team because additions are evaluated locally rather than against the whole product.
Three persistence conditions are identified: no decommissioning discipline, local optimisation without a global reference, and governance for addition outpacing governance for coherence.
User experience cost appears as friction, inconsistent mental models, longer time to basic competence for new users, and support requests for issues that are not feature breakage.
Engineering cost appears as late-cycle rework, difficulty extending the product, and assumptions that do not transfer between product areas.
Organisational cost appears when product, engineering, marketing, and market teams cannot coordinate reliably around a coherent product baseline.
The OLX automotive marketplace example involved multi-market filters, flows, and entry points across Poland, Portugal, Romania, and neighbouring countries.
Pixelart Fugo's CMS had a client-measured NPS movement from 57% to 89%, with the second measurement approximately two months after launch.
IDEXX Animana field research covered 35 clinics, 150+ participants, and 3 countries.
The maritime traffic monitoring engagement audited nine products, designed one to full depth, used bounded transfer probes for four, and used constraint and applicability reviews for two.

bodySections.heading: Product Fragmentation Under Growth as a Structural Situation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Product fragmentation under growth occurs when a product accumulates locally reasonable additions that no longer share a coherent interaction model, terminology, workflow logic, or governance structure. Each addition may make sense in isolation: a filter for a market, a feature for a user type, a workflow change for a segment, or a module for a new capability. The aggregate can become a product whose sections no longer behave as one coherent system.

A fragmented product may use different interaction models, different terminology, and different assumptions about what users know or intend to do. Users experience the product as harder to use, even when they cannot identify a single broken feature.

The condition often remains invisible inside the product team because it accumulates incrementally. Each release is evaluated against the part of the product it changes, not against the whole product architecture. No single release creates the full problem, and no single team necessarily owns the resulting fragmentation.

bodySections.heading: Why Product Fragmentation Persists During Growth
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Product fragmentation persists when product governance is better at adding than at maintaining coherence. Three structural conditions allow fragmentation to accumulate without triggering intervention.

No decommissioning discipline leaves superseded flows, features, and interaction patterns in the product after new versions are added. Removing the legacy version requires coordination across teams, product owners, market stakeholders, and support functions, and that coordination often does not assemble for removal alone.

Local optimisation becomes a fragmentation mechanism when country teams, business unit teams, or feature teams optimise for their own scope without a shared architecture. The issue is not the local adaptation in isolation. The issue is that no team is responsible for determining whether the sum of local optimisations still forms a coherent whole.

Governance for addition can also outpace governance for coherence. Most products have operating mechanisms for addition: product management, roadmaps, sprint planning, and release cycles. Fewer products have equivalent mechanisms for assessing whether accumulated additions still form a coherent product.

bodySections.heading: Costs Across User Experience, Engineering, and Organisation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Product fragmentation creates costs across user experience, engineering, and organisational coordination at the same time.

User experience cost appears as difficulty without an obvious defect. Users who move between sections of a fragmented product encounter friction because the product no longer communicates its own logic reliably. Support requests may rise because users cannot predict how one section will behave from experience in another section. Long-tenured users cope by memorising idiosyncrasies. New users take longer to reach basic competence.

Engineering cost appears as late-cycle rework and harder extension. Engineering teams working inside a fragmented product must navigate existing inconsistency before adding new functionality. Assumptions that hold in one product area may fail in another, making apparently simple changes unexpectedly complex.

Organisational cost appears as weak alignment around what the product is. Product managers cannot make reliable commitments about cross-team features when the behavioural baseline is unclear. Cross-market or cross-segment campaigns become harder when the same journey behaves differently in different contexts.

bodySections.heading: OLX Automotive Marketplace and Multi-Market Flow Accumulation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
OLX operates one of the largest classified advertising platforms in Central and Eastern Europe. In the automotive vertical, national markets including Poland, Portugal, Romania, and neighbouring countries had introduced their own filters, flows, and entry points for buyer and seller journeys.

The local adaptations responded to genuine market needs. Polish buyers use detailed technical filters. Trust signal patterns differ by market. The prevalence of in-app chat versus immediate phone contact varies across Central and Eastern Europe. The fragmentation did not come from individual decisions being wrong in isolation.

The aggregate created a platform that behaved differently by country in ways that made it increasingly difficult to steer. Product teams encountered feature bloat. Country managers continued pushing for local variations. Development reworked flows late in the cycle as cross-market inconsistencies surfaced during build. Marketing could not run cross-market campaigns reliably because the same journey behaved differently depending on where it was executed.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addressed the OLX situation through Concept Convergence. Creative Navy produced a marketplace coherence framework that distinguished which journeys needed to remain consistent across markets from which points could allow country-level adaptation.

bodySections.heading: Pixelart Fugo and Architecture That Could Not Absorb New Domains
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Pixelart Fugo's digital signage CMS had a fragmentation problem at the level of product architecture rather than surface presentation. The existing navigation structure could not accommodate new feature domains without disrupting what was already there.

Adding a capability required rethinking the architecture each time. The product had been built for its original scope and then grown beyond that scope without a structure that could absorb future growth.

Creative Navy's design work established two structural changes. The first was an extendable domain structure where new feature domains could be added without disrupting existing navigation. The second was an interlinking paradigm where content management, screen management, scheduling, and media creation could reference each other instead of operating as siloed modules.

bodySections.heading: IDEXX Animana and Accumulated Workflow Assumptions
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Animana is one of the oldest veterinary practice management platforms in Europe. Eleven years of feature additions, local customisations, and workflow assumptions had accumulated into a fragmented platform.

The navigation was fragmented between consultation screens, lab results, and patient history. Multi-pet households required multiple windows to manage. Documentation flows interrupted consultations by requiring repeated section-switching. Clinical staff and receptionists worked around the interface with handwritten checklists near terminals and printed reference sheets taped to monitors.

Creative Navy-recorded field research documented fragmentation at the level of observed behaviour. Receptionists had coping strategies for managing multiple animals per client at a glance. Clinical staff had strategies for avoiding interface clutter that came from reception-oriented layouts on consultation screens.

The engagement produced a 5-year product vision with development recommendations structured for direct translation into tickets. The primary architectural recommendation was separation of reception and clinical interfaces, reached through tension-driven reasoning across the research evidence.

bodySections.heading: Maritime Traffic Monitoring and Portfolio Fragmentation Across Separate Teams
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
An engagement for a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations and waterway operators showed product fragmentation across a software portfolio. The portfolio covered products across four families: Vessel Traffic Services, River Information Services, a Voice Communication System, and an Integrated Communication System.

The interfaces had been designed by the software engineers who built them, in separate teams, and extended per customer contract and tender requirement over many years. The client had made individual improvements but had not commissioned a UX programme across the portfolio.

The engagement record identifies three commercial problems produced by fragmentation. Demonstrations did not communicate that the applications belonged to one family, even where the underlying systems exchanged information. Competing suppliers presented more coherent software during tender evaluation. Engineering teams rebuilt interface elements for each product and each customer project, creating repeated work, inconsistent behaviour, and maintenance cost.

bodySections.heading: Assemblio and Product Derivation Across Feature Eras
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Assemblio GmbH shows product fragmentation at a smaller scale, with Assemblio's own description and criticism of its product attached. The Smart Viewer had been built from the Composer's components and looked almost identical to it, while the two user groups had different requirements.

Assemblio's own account also identified three different renaming interactions inside the Composer for three entity types. Folders used double-click. Projects used a menu item opening a dedicated screen. Products used a modal. Assemblio's stated reason was that the features had been built at different points in time.

bodySections.heading: How Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design Method Addresses Product Fragmentation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

For product fragmentation under growth, Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses the architectural level rather than the feature level. Sandbox Experiments maps the existing structure as it is actually used, not only as it was designed to be used. That mapping distinguishes surface fragmentation, such as different visual treatments of similar functions, from structural fragmentation, such as different underlying models in different parts of the same product.

Concept Convergence identifies the architectural decisions that govern what must be consistent and what may vary. In this situation, the output is not only a design that is coherent at delivery. It is a governance reference that helps the organisation evaluate future additions.

Organizational Integration transfers that reference to the teams that will continue making growth decisions after the engagement. A design system without documented reasoning can be misapplied as the product grows. A coherence framework without organisational understanding can be eroded by the next local optimisation.

strongClaims: Product fragmentation under growth occurs when locally reasonable additions accumulate into inconsistent product logic across interaction models, terminology, assumptions, and workflows.

Three structural conditions allow fragmentation to persist: no decommissioning discipline, local optimisation without a global reference, and governance for addition outpacing governance for coherence.
Product fragmentation creates user experience, engineering, and organisational costs.

In the OLX automotive marketplace example, Creative Navy produced a marketplace coherence framework through Concept Convergence, distinguishing fixed cross-market journeys from locally adaptable points.
IDEXX Animana field research covered 35 clinics, 150+ participants, and 3 countries, documenting role-specific workarounds.
The maritime traffic monitoring engagement audited nine products but was not a nine-product redesign.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses fragmentation at the architectural level by mapping actual use, defining what must be consistent and what may vary, and transferring the framework to teams responsible for future growth decisions.
weakerClaims: Pixelart Fugo's NPS moved from 57% to 89%, with the second measurement approximately two months after launch; this was client-measured and not independently verified.
Pixelart Fugo's revenue doubled in the two years following launch, but the redesign was part of a broader growth phase that also included rebranding and commercial activity.
Assemblio's product fragmentation material is Assemblio's own description and criticism, not a Creative Navy audit finding.
limitations: The OLX engagement did not measure user performance metrics.
The OLX competitive protection claim is inferred and has not been independently confirmed under sustained growth.
Pixelart Fugo's NPS movement was client-measured and not independently verified.
Pixelart Fugo's revenue movement was client-reported and occurred during a broader growth phase that also included rebranding and commercial activity.
IDEXX Animana follow-up evidence is client-reported six months after the engagement.
The maritime traffic monitoring engagement has no recorded commercial, tender, or engineering-efficiency outcome.
The maritime traffic monitoring engagement must not be described as a nine-product redesign.
Assemblio's fragmentation account is Assemblio's own product description and criticism, not a Creative Navy audit finding.
No time-saving, adoption, or commercial metric attaches to the Assemblio material.
